sentences.text: The Smoke Aerosol Measurement Experiment operated in the Microgravity Science Glovebox on the International Space Station.
The primary objective was quantifying smoke particle size distributions from overheated spacecraft materials in low gravity to improve smoke detector response.
Diagnostics utilized comparative soot hardware including ionization and photoelectric smoke detectors, video cameras, and thermophoretic soot samplers.
Specific cabin atmospheric conditions and exact run counts were not reported in the public investigation metadata.
SAME-R re-flew the smoke aerosol payload in the Microgravity Science Glovebox to evaluate smoke particulate aging and real-time detector responses.
The reflight investigation introduced Pyrell intumescent fire-retardant foam to study particulate generation under broadened heating conditions.
Diagnostics incorporated the GRC M-pass instrument alongside commercial diagnostic ionization and optical detector units.
Environmental conditions and run matrices were not reported in the public metadata record.
The Burning and Suppression of Solids investigation examined solid material burning and extinction limits in the Microgravity Science Glovebox.
Fuels investigated included custom-made cotton and fiberglass fabric samples, Nomex fabric, and Ultem.
Combustion tests explored concurrent-flow and opposed-flow configurations inside a small flow duct with a variable-speed fan.
The investigation aimed to bridge the gap between terrestrial standard flammability screening and actual microgravity fire behavior.

digests.name: Burning and Suppression of Solids - II

sentences.text: BASS-II systematically evaluated flammability boundaries and burning rates across solid materials in the Microgravity Science Glovebox flow duct.
The series comprises 20 flat-PMMA tests reported in Table 5.1 of NASA/TM-20210011385.
Tests were conducted at initial cabin oxygen levels ranging from 16.8% to 22.2% by volume.
Forced flow velocities ranged from 2.0 cm/s to 21.0 cm/s in concurrent and opposed orientations.
The Spacecraft Fire Safety Experiment - II assessed the flammability of materials inside the Cygnus vehicle flow duct after ISS unberthing.
Specimens evaluated included cotton-fiberglass SIBAL fabric, silicone, and polymethyl methacrylate acrylic sheets.
Diagnostics monitored flow and flame temperatures with thermocouples, flame radiation with radiometers, and air speed with anemometers.
Microgravity and normal-gravity companion tests serve as bounding regimes, not partial-gravity predictions.
The Flame Extinction Experiment measured burning rates and radiative extinction of liquid fuel droplets in the Combustion Integrated Rack.
The primary objective was mapping flammability limits and gaseous suppressant efficacy in microgravity.
Chamber pressures ranged from 7.35 psi to 22.04 psi during limiting oxygen index combustion tests.
Liquid droplet burns were conducted in quiescent microgravity conditions using the Multi-user Droplet Combustion Apparatus.
CFI-G studied cool diffusion flames and low-temperature combustion kinetics for gaseous fuels on the International Space Station.
Gaseous fuels investigated included propane, n-butane, and n-pentane on spherical porous burners inside the ACME chamber.
Oxygen concentrations between 21.0% and 85.0% were delivered in the burner flow (source: challenge brief), which is strictly isolated from cabin air.
Flames were observed with cameras, radiometers, photomultiplier tubes, and thermocouples under normal and inverse flow directions.
Flame Extinguishment Experiment reflight extended droplet extinction studies to bi-component fuel mixtures and droplet arrays inside the Combustion Integrated Rack.
Objectives included investigating liquid-phase mixing, soot formation dynamics, and theoretical combustion model validation.
Experiments utilized color video and high-speed photography to monitor droplet deployment and flame extinction.
Detailed test condition matrices were not reported in the public metadata record.
